note: SPOILERS. Text for the hidden things.

rows.text: At the foot of the dead tree there is a very small door, locked, with a very small doormat. Wipe your feet, it suggests.
A canoe with a hole in it. A name is painted on the bow, crossed out, and a better name painted underneath: STILL FLOATS (MOSTLY).
Under the lean-to, a biscuit tin of supplies, and a note: Take what you need. Leave something for the next ranger.
One large, slow ripple crosses the pond from one side to the other. Then nothing. The water is perfectly still.
A survey stake with a faded ribbon. Someone has written on it: TOWER, THIS WAY. KEEP GOING. The writing gets less tidy the further you go.
Seven ordinary mushrooms in a perfect circle. Just mushrooms. Probably.
A boulder shaped very much like a sleeping bear. Very much. It might be snoring.
Carved in the bark: RANGER WAS HERE. And under it, in a different hand: SO WAS I.
The lookout's tally book. Smokes spotted: 0. Lights spotted: 214.
Day one. The tower radio works if you thump it. It's a good radio, if a little ahead of itself. Weather tomorrow: fine, it says. I'll let you know. - R.
A mossy stone bench, facing a blank rock wall, as if there were a view. It's quite a nice wall.
An old park truck, rusted solid, with a tree growing up through the bonnet. The keys are still in it.
BRIDGE TOLLS, says the board. Every price has been scratched out. Small pawprints in the mud lead out onto the bridge and stop at the gap.
A tunnel through the blackberry thicket, far too low for a person, worn smooth by something.
Journal page
Odd things noticed: {n}.
Fished from the dock at first light. One big, slow ripple went right across the pond. No fish that size. Probably.
Woke early. The whole pond rippled once, like something rolling over in its sleep. Then nothing.
Who was on the radio up in the tower last night? Lovely voice. Read out the weather for tomorrow, very politely.
[A drawing of a rusty old truck with a tree growing out of it. The truck has a face. It is smiling.]
Take it up
The old bench comes apart in your hands. One plank is still good.
Fish it out
A trail sign, waterlogged but sound. It'll stand again.
Sweep the doormat
You sweep the very small doormat with great care.
Right the stake
You work the stake out of the ash and set it straight. The ribbon flutters.
Set a mushroom in the gap
Seven again. The ring looks easier, somehow.
Knock the glovebox open
One good knock and the glovebox drops open. Papers, and a rattle of old pencils.
Ease the nest out
An old nest, long empty. You set it in a tree nearby, just in case.
Take up the old bench (hammer)
Put out a new bench at the outlook
A New Seat at the Outlook
Bench at the outlook's rotten through. Worth a new one.
Fish the sign out of the ford
Put it up as a pointer at the ford
The Sign in the Ford
Old sign in the ford. Somebody's been missing it.
Sweep the tiny doormat
Thanks, probably.
Sweep the Tiny Doormat
Tiny door's got a tiny note on it now: DOORMAT WANTS SWEEPING.
Pick up 6 litter round the lean-to
Tidy the Lean-to
Somebody's been camping rough at the lean-to. Bit of a mess.
Right the fallen stake
Build a cairn beside it
Right the Middle Stake
Middle stake's down. The ribbon's still tied on. Hate to lose it.
Set 1 mushroom in the gap in the ring
The Seventh Mushroom
Mushroom ring's got a gap. Seven before, six now. I'd swear it.
Knock the glovebox open with the hammer
A page of the last ranger's journal, folded in the glovebox: "Truck died here. Walked the rest. Better that way, honestly."
The Truck's Glovebox
Glovebox on the old truck's stuck shut. Something rattles.
Clear the nest from the chimney
Clear the Cabin Chimney
Cabin stove smokes. Something's nesting in the chimney.
Be on the beach between 6:00 and 6:30 on another clear morning
Survey there
Lines in the Sand
Left a line in the sand last night. This morning there's a second line beside it.
Behind a loose board: a chipped mug, painted with a moose. It's still warm.
When you look back, someone has neatened the letters on your sign.
Tonight, the radio reads tomorrow's forecast before tomorrow comes.
Under the static, someone is humming. It stops when you listen.
Someone's left something on the step. Small someone.
The lookout's log has a new tally mark in it. Not in your hand.
A mitten, far too small for anyone you know of.
Someone lit the stove before you got here. The kindling is stacked neater than you do it.
Something has walked your trail already. It seemed to like it.
The last stake has a new ribbon. You didn't tie it.
The badger has left you a bottle cap. Possibly an apology.
Overnight, someone's carved a letter into the bench.
On the back, faded: THIS WAY, MOSTLY.
A key the size of a fingernail, left on the doormat.
Written on the ribbon, in pencil: "If you're reading this, you came the long way. Good."
That night, the ring glows. Just the once.
The truck's logbook. The last entry has a date and nothing else.
A third line now. Then the pond laps over them all.

Once, a fire tower keeper lived up on the ridge all year, and every night they counted the lights on the lake. Some nights there were seven, some nights seventy. They wrote every number in a book. People in town said, "Aren't you lonely up there?" And the keeper said, "Lonely? I've never had so much company." When they came down at last, the book was full, and every page ended the same way: "All present."

There was a winter so long the creek forgot how to run. A girl from Humdrum walked out on the ice to the middle of the lake, because her grandmother said the lake had something to tell her. She lay down and put her ear to the ice. She never said what she heard. But that spring the creek ran early, and she grew up to be a librarian. Not me. Probably not me.

They say the pines in the park were planted by someone walking backwards, so nobody could follow their footsteps. That's why the trails curl. That's why you always come back to where you started, if you walk long enough. It isn't getting lost, the old folk said. It's being shown round twice.

A ranger once left their lantern burning on the outlook all night, by mistake. In the morning there was a ring of footprints in the frost around it, all facing in, as if a crowd had stood very quietly to look at it, and then gone home. The ranger left a lantern there every winter after that. Just in case they wanted to come back.

My mother told me the park keeps a list. Not of the people who come in, but of the people who come back. Every time you walk through the gate again, your name goes a little higher. She said that's why the gate creaks. It's writing.
The tower's tune
The radio played it all the way through. Teo would know it.
The badgers wait. What will you offer, each week?
A tin of beans each week
Churros each week
Your old boots, once (good for a season)
Agreed: {item}. They nod, gravely.
The deal was {item}.
They're not morning badgers. Leave it at dusk.
They've had this week's.
You leave it on the stone with the lid off. Something rustles, approvingly.
They'd follow something they love.
They'll eat this one tonight. The next spot tomorrow.
Trail spot {n} of {of} laid.
An empty hook by the door. Something used to hang here.
The little bell hangs on its hook again.
You hang the bell on its hook. It rings once, softly, on its own.
Behind the tower's radio, wrapped in a rag: a small brass bell, and a label in the last ranger's hand. "Yard. Back soon."
An old list pinned under the others, in the last ranger's hand: "Bell: lent to tower (temp.)"
In the night, the bell rang once. You slept well.
The deer walks to the door, touches the bell with its nose, and it rings. It lies down by the step and stays till dawn.
Something that rang in your yard is missing. Things that ring want to be heard.
Oh! Hello. Sorry. I'm Gord. I'm usually... taller. Lower. Anyway. I was wondering, and you can say no: how does a person go into town and have a coffee? Like a normal person. Just once.
Evening! Lovely moon. I've been practising standing.
No rush. There's always another full moon. That's the one thing I can count on.
I did think about clothes. I have these. Are these enough? They feel like not enough.
Gord practises ordering. You're Wren. What do you say?
"Morning! What can I get you?"
"Next!"
"You're a moose."
"A... coffee, please. Black. Thank you. Thank YOU." He's beaming. "Again?"
He jumps a little. "Coffee! Please! Sorry!" Then, quietly: "I'll get better."
"I'm Gord," he says, very firmly. Then he laughs, and it's fine.
Tonight? Tonight. Right. I'm ready. I'll walk behind you. Is that normal? I'll walk beside you.
Same again next month, I think. I have a usual now. Do you know what that's like?

The bell over the door. Gord ducks under it. Wren looks up.

"Evening! What can I get you?"

"A coffee," says Gord. "Black. Please."

She pours it. He holds it in both hands. Someone by the window says, "Evening," and goes back to their paper.

Gord sits down very carefully and looks at you as if you'd hung the moon.
Wren laughs. "Easy. You say what you want and please, and I say what it costs. Want to try?" You don't say who it's for. She doesn't ask.
"Stay open late? On the full moon?" Wren thinks. "For you, sure. Day {day}. I'll put a sign out."
Wren smiles. "Late? I hardly know you." (She'll stay open late for a friend.)
Under the aurora the tower's radio stops hissing and plays a tune, clearly, all the way through. Then the static comes back.
The badgers have made you something: a hat of leaves. They hold a very short ceremony. You are now, it seems, an honorary badger.
One of the jackalopes followed you home and is asleep in the pet's bed. The pet is appalled, then isn't.
At dawn the deer leads you to the outlook and stands beside you while the sun comes up. Nothing else happens. That's the point.
"I knew someone who worked in this park," Gord says. "Wore a hat like yours." He doesn't say who.
